summary: Describes GREASE, a mechanism to prevent extensibility failures in the TLS ecosystem. It reserves a set of TLS values that clients and servers may advertise so that peers keep correctly handling unknown values instead of breaking when new ones appear.

plainLanguage.summary: GREASE uses reserved TLS values to test whether peers tolerate values they do not recognize. This can reveal compatibility problems before new TLS features depend on that behavior.

questions: why does tls reserve random values
subtitle: Reserved TLS values that test whether implementations tolerate unknown values

tldr.problem: TLS extensibility depends on implementations ignoring unknown values. An implementation that rejects unknown values can continue working with existing peers, hiding the bug until new values are deployed.
tldr.mechanism: GREASE reserves unused values that implementations may advertise at random. Peers must handle them as unknown values and must not negotiate them.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism exposes implementations that reject unknown values before those failures interfere with deployment of new TLS features.

facts.label: Reserved cipher suite and ALPN values

today: RFC 8701 is an Informational document and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It reserves GREASE values for testing TLS handling of unknown values.

sections.title: Preventing TLS Extensibility Failures
sections.content:
TLS lets one peer advertise capabilities, such as cipher suites and extensions, for another peer to select. The receiving implementation must ignore unknown values so new capabilities can be introduced without breaking interoperability.

A bug that rejects unknown values can remain hidden while implementations communicate using known values. When a new value is introduced, the peer may fail. GREASE reserves unused values for implementations to advertise so this behavior can be tested before it blocks deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS peers need to accept values they do not recognize. GREASE checks this behavior by sending reserved values before new features depend on it.

sections.title: The Reserved Values
sections.content:
The RFC reserves sixteen values for cipher suites and ALPN identifiers, using two-byte patterns from {0x0A,0x0A} through {0xFA,0xFA}. It reserves sixteen related values for extensions, named groups, signature algorithms, and versions, from 0x0A0A through 0xFAFA.

It also reserves eight values for PskKeyExchangeModes: 0x0B, 0x2A, 0x49, 0x68, 0x87, 0xA6, 0xC5, and 0xE4. The reserved version values are no longer available for TLS or DTLS version numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets aside patterns of values for several TLS lists. These values are reserved for testing how peers handle unknown entries.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A client MAY advertise GREASE values in ClientHello fields such as cipher suites, extensions, supported groups, signature algorithms, supported versions, PskKeyExchangeModes, and ALPN identifiers. Servers MUST treat them like other unknown values, MUST NOT negotiate them, and MUST try remaining parameters.

Servers may also advertise GREASE values in certain TLS 1.3 CertificateRequest and NewSessionTicket fields. Clients must ignore these as unknown values and must not negotiate them. If a peer selects a GREASE value where a negotiated value is expected, the other side must fail the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A client or server may include GREASE values where the protocol allows them. The other side must ignore them as unknown and must never select one.

sections.title: Choosing GREASE Values
sections.content:
Implementations advertising GREASE values SHOULD select them at random. This encourages peers to ignore unknown values generally rather than recognizing only one reserved value. Implementations must still follow normal protocol rules, including rules against duplicate extension types in one extension block.

The RFC recommends balancing variation with predictable testing. Changing GREASE positions on every connection may make a failure intermittent and allow retries to hide it. Keeping positions stable for a period, such as a software release, tests fewer cases but can expose failures more reliably in those cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Random selection encourages peers to handle unknown values generally. Implementations should also avoid making failures so intermittent that automatic retries hide them.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
GREASE values cannot be negotiated, so the RFC says they do not directly affect TLS connection security. GREASE can reduce the need to retry a failed connection with a new feature disabled, a fallback that an active attacker could trigger to suppress the feature.

Implementations SHOULD NOT retry with GREASE disabled after connection failure. If GREASE values are not selected at random, their pattern may identify an implementation or individual user, creating a privacy risk.
sections.plainLanguage: GREASE values are not negotiated, but retries that disable GREASE could hide compatibility failures. A predictable GREASE pattern may also make a client easier to identify.
